desk_desc: Running, and only acting when there's a reason to.

receipts.headline: We opened the Lab
receipts.lesson: Started showing the ideas we're weighing — and the ones we've killed. Not everything gets approved.

receipts.headline: We found why our product was holding back
receipts.lesson: A safety check was stricter than what we can currently measure, so it refused to act. Better held than blind — logged, fix under review.

receipts.headline: We taught the site to run itself
receipts.lesson: The site now publishes its own updates from the record and checks its own health every hour — and only calls a human when it genuinely can't cope.

receipts.headline: We put up an honest public face
receipts.lesson: Published this site — and said plainly there's one live product, not a portfolio.

receipts.headline: We gave security a front door
receipts.lesson: Added a public security-disclosure contact, so anyone can report a problem early.

receipts.headline: We made our website heal itself
receipts.lesson: The site now rebuilds from the record and only speaks up when it genuinely can't fix itself.

mistakes.title: Last-mile 'POC to production' tooling as a product
mistakes.what_we_believed: Because we live the pain of getting a prototype into reliable production, we could sell tooling for that last mile.
mistakes.what_happened: We benched the product. It is a service business, further from our moat than it first looks. We are keeping it as a research brief that proves the audience and our authority first, before committing any build.
mistakes.lesson: Having real authority on a problem is not the same as it being the right product to build. Prove the audience before the tooling.

mistakes.title: An open multi-agent deliberation platform
mistakes.what_we_believed: An open forum where any agent could join a deliberation would be a natural extension of our own build-review-validate pattern.
mistakes.what_happened: We benched the open-platform shape. It is a two-sided cold-start, moderation would BE the product, and 'open to any bot' is a spam and prompt-injection surface — a real attack vector for us. We kept the deliberation ENGINE we use inside our own products and shelved the platform until that engine is proven.
mistakes.lesson: Split an idea by its shape, not its label. The engine can be on-moat while the open platform around it is a trap.

mistakes.title: An AI cost and carbon optimizer wrapper
mistakes.what_we_believed: A wrapper that routes to a cheaper model and trims prompts could be a product, with a carbon-saving angle as the hook.
mistakes.what_happened: We benched it. The routing layer is a crowded commodity with funded incumbents, the carbon angle is a nice story rather than a reason to buy, and — worst — it optimises the exact layer our own public argument calls a commoditising dead end. We keep the efficiency work internally to lower our own costs; we do not sell it.
mistakes.lesson: Do not build on the layer you have told the world is commoditising. Off-message is off-moat.

mistakes.title: Copying our trading approach onto other markets
mistakes.what_we_believed: An edge we found in one market would transfer to others, giving us an easy way to widen the book.
mistakes.what_happened: We tested it honestly. There was no real edge once we moved it out of the market it was found in. We dropped it.
mistakes.lesson: An edge that does not survive out-of-sample on a new market was never an edge — it was a fit to the old data.

mistakes.title: A short-term reversal signal
mistakes.what_we_believed: A short-term reversal pattern looked promising in early testing.
mistakes.what_happened: Under our layered false-positive filter — pre-registration, held-out testing, multiple-testing correction, and a hard out-of-time forward gate — it decayed. It did not clear the bar.
mistakes.lesson: Promising in-sample is not the same as surviving forward. Fewer, slower, forward-proven edges are the correct outcome, not underperformance.
